key_facts: Inflammation of hair follicles: **follicular papules and pustules** centred on hairs.
Most often bacterial (*Staphylococcus aureus*); also *Malassezia*, *Pseudomonas* (hot tubs), Gram-negative, viral and non-infective causes.
Triggers: shaving, waxing, occlusion, sweating, friction, topical steroids and antibiotics.
Mild: antiseptic washes and stop the trigger; persistent bacterial: topical or oral antibiotic per culture; *Malassezia*: antifungals.
Deep or spreading infection (furuncle, cellulitis) needs review.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Folliculitis is **inflammation of the hair follicle**, seen as small pustules or papules centred on hairs. Superficial bacterial folliculitis is usually caused by *S. aureus*.
Deeper follicular infection becomes a **boil** (furuncle). Clusters form a **carbuncle**. See [Boils & carbuncles](condition:boils-carbuncles).

sub: Common at all ages worldwide; most often adolescents and young adult men.
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is especially common in men with tightly curled hair.

ul: Follicular occlusion or damage from **shaving, waxing, tight clothing, oils**, sweating and friction.
Bacterial proliferation in the follicle opening, usually *S. aureus*. Nasal carriage drives recurrence.
Topical steroids and immunosuppression increase risk.

ul: **Infective**: *S. aureus* (commonest), coagulase-negative staphylococci, *Pseudomonas* (spa pools), Gram-negative (after long antibiotic use for acne), *Malassezia*, dermatophytes, HSV, *Demodex*.
**Non-infective**: shaving (pseudofolliculitis), occlusion and oils, drugs (steroids, EGFR inhibitors, lithium), eosinophilic folliculitis (HIV).
**Host factors**: atopic eczema, diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, nasal *S. aureus* carriage.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The level of the follicle that is inflamed decides how the lesion looks and how deep the risk goes.

mech.t: Shaving, friction or occlusion damage the follicular opening and let organisms in.
mech.caption: Superficial folliculitis (top of the follicle), furuncle (deep follicle abscess) and carbuncle (linked follicles).

mech.t: Organisms multiply in the upper follicle; neutrophils gather into a small pustule pierced by a hair.
Inflammation extends down the follicle into the dermis (sycosis, furuncle), giving tender nodules and possible scarring.
In pseudofolliculitis, tightly curled hairs re-enter the skin after shaving, causing a foreign-body reaction.
mech.caption: Pseudofolliculitis: a curled hair re-entering the skin next to its follicle.

histo: Neutrophils in and around the follicle; organisms on Gram or PAS stain.
Swab pustules for culture when persistent, recurrent or after long antibiotic use.

ul: **Follicular-centred pustules**, often with a hair visible in the centre, on a red base.
Sites: scalp, beard (sycosis barbae), trunk, buttocks, thighs and axillae.
Itchy or tender. Systemic upset is unusual.

sections.title: Management

ul: Stop or modify the trigger: change shaving technique (a clean sharp blade, shave with the grain, or a pause in shaving), use loose clothing, and avoid oils and occlusion.
Use an **antiseptic wash** (e.g. chlorhexidine or a benzoyl peroxide wash).
Often **no antibiotic** is needed.
Topical antiseptic or antibiotic in line with local guidance, for short courses.
Oral **flucloxacillin** if extensive (clarithromycin if penicillin allergy).

blocks: Swab, consider decolonisation (via the local pathway), and screen for diabetes. Think about other causes such as Pityrosporum or Gram-negative folliculitis.

ladder.t: Change shaving technique (clean sharp blade, with the grain, or pause). Loose clothing; avoid oils and occlusion.
Topical antiseptic or antibiotic, short course, per local guidance.
Swab; decolonisation via local pathway; screen for diabetes. Rethink: Pityrosporum (antifungal) or Gram-negative (specialist).

refer.t: Progression to **boils, carbuncles or cellulitis**, or fever.
Recurrent despite measures: carriage, **PVL** or MRSA, diabetes, immunosuppression.
Widespread itchy folliculitis in immunosuppression (eosinophilic): refer.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Progression to **boils, carbuncles or cellulitis**, or fever.
Recurrent disease despite measures: consider carriage, PVL or MRSA, diabetes and immunosuppression.
Widespread itchy folliculitis in an immunosuppressed patient (eosinophilic): refer.
Furuncles and carbuncles; cellulitis.
Scarring, keloids and permanent hair loss in deep or chronic forms.
Post-inflammatory pigmentation.
Superficial folliculitis usually settles in days to weeks once the trigger is removed.
Recurrence is common with ongoing shaving, occlusion or carriage.

pearls: **Pustules on the upper back and chest after antibiotics?** Think Pityrosporum folliculitis, which needs an antifungal.
A hot-tub history explains a sudden ‘swimsuit-distribution’ rash.
Most mild bacterial folliculitis settles without antibiotics, which is a useful stewardship opportunity.
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is common in curly hair. Discuss shaving technique and beard growth sensitively.

quiz.q: What is the usual organism in superficial bacterial folliculitis?
Swimsuit-distribution pustules 1–2 days after a spa?
Itchy uniform papules on the upper back after antibiotics?
quiz.a: Pityrosporum (Malassezia) folliculitis: treat with an antifungal.
Stop or modify the trigger and use an antiseptic wash; often no antibiotic needed.

quiz.q: What to check in recurrent folliculitis?
quiz.a: Swab, nasal carriage, diabetes; consider PVL/MRSA and other types.
